planting.note: Divide and replant in early spring as new growth emerges, or in fall once flowering has finished.

directions: Alba bears pale greenish-white pincushion flowerheads ringed by papery, faintly green-tinged bracts, giving a cooler, more luminous presence in the border than the pink and wine-toned forms of the species. Plant divisions into humus-rich, evenly moist soil in a spot with morning sun and afternoon shade, which keeps the stems upright and the flower color crisp rather than washed out. Shear spent flower stems back after the first bloom cycle to tidy the clump and often coax a lighter second flush into early fall. Established clumps resent prolonged dryness, so mulch to conserve moisture through summer, and divide every three to four years to maintain vigor.

planting.note: Set divisions out in early spring or early fall into cool, moisture-retentive soil.

directions: Rubra carries rose-red pincushion flowerheads surrounded by matching red-flushed bracts from early summer through fall, giving one of the richest and longest-lasting color displays among the greater masterworts. It tolerates wetter ground than most Astrantia selections and performs especially well along streamsides or in low spots that stay consistently damp. Grow in part shade with organically rich soil, and deadhead the earliest flush to prevent excessive self-seeding while prompting continued bloom. Lift and divide crowded clumps every few years in early spring, replanting divisions promptly so the fibrous roots do not dry out.

common_name: Oxford Blue Sea Holly (Deep-Blue Pyrenean Eryngo)

planting.note: Transplant once soil has warmed, siting the deep taproot where it will not need to be moved again.

directions: Oxford Blue produces an especially saturated, deep indigo-blue flower cone surrounded by silvery-blue spiny bracts, a richer and darker tone than most seedling-raised bourgatii selections. The deeply cut, silver-veined basal foliage stays attractive through most of the season even before bloom. Site it in lean, sharply drained, gritty soil in full sun, since fertile or damp ground produces lax growth and dulls both bract color and leaf variegation. Leave the taproot undisturbed once planted and avoid winter mulch directly over the crown, which can trap moisture and rot the roots in cold, wet winters.

planting.note: Plant divisions or pot-grown stock in spring once the soil has warmed and dried out from winter wet.

directions: This naturally occurring hybrid sea holly, of uncertain parentage but widely grown for its vivid steely-blue flower stems, produces branching cone-shaped flowerheads ringed by narrow, metallic-blue spiny bracts above coarsely toothed, heart-shaped basal leaves. It grows taller and more robust than many of its Eryngium relatives, forming an architectural clump that holds its color from midsummer well into fall. Give it full sun and sharply drained soil, since the long taproot is prone to rot in heavy or waterlogged ground over winter. Established plants are long-lived and need little attention beyond an occasional cutback of old flower stems; bees visit the flowers heavily throughout bloom.
